lesson.title: Who Gets to Stay: America's Immigration Debates
lesson.summary: Modern immigration debates trace back to the 1965 law that reshaped who could come to America, and remain unresolved as Congress has repeatedly failed to pass comprehensive reform balancing enforcement, humanitarian obligations, and economic needs.
lesson.body:
American immigration debates in the twenty first century build directly on a policy foundation laid decades earlier. The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also called the Hart Celler Act, eliminated the national origins quota system that had been in place since the 1920s and had strongly favored immigrants from Northern and Western Europe. In its place, the 1965 law created a system prioritizing family reunification and, to a lesser degree, needed job skills. Lawmakers at the time did not expect the change to dramatically shift immigration patterns, but it led, over the following decades, to a substantial and sustained increase in immigration from Asia, Latin America, and Africa, reshaping the demographic makeup of the United States.

Immigration policy continued to evolve after 1965. The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, signed by President Reagan, combined a path to legal status for an estimated three million undocumented immigrants already in the country with new penalties for employers who knowingly hired undocumented workers, an approach intended to combine enforcement with a practical solution for people already settled in the country. Undocumented immigration, particularly across the U.S. Mexico border, continued to rise in the following decades, and after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, immigration enforcement became more closely tied to national security, leading to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security in 2002 and increased border security spending.

In more recent decades, immigration policy has become one of the more polarized issues in American politics. In 2012, the Obama administration created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, known as DACA, through executive action, allowing certain undocumented immigrants who had been brought to the United States as children, often called Dreamers, to receive renewable protection from deportation and permission to work, without providing a permanent path to citizenship, which would require an act of Congress. The Trump administration announced in 2017 that it would end DACA, leading to extended litigation, and in 2020 the Supreme Court ruled in DHS v. Regents of the University of California that the administration's method of ending the program was legally improper, allowing it to continue. Trump's first term also included a travel ban restricting entry from several majority Muslim countries, expanded construction of barriers along the southern border, and, in 2018, a short lived zero tolerance policy that resulted in the separation of migrant families at the border, a policy that drew significant bipartisan criticism and was formally ended after public backlash. Title 42, a public health authority invoked during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, was used by both the Trump and Biden administrations to rapidly expel many migrants at the border without standard asylum processing, until it was lifted in 2023.

Immigration debates today center on a recurring set of tensions rather than settled answers. Supporters of more open immigration policies point to economic contributions from immigrant labor, family reunification values embedded in the 1965 law, and humanitarian obligations toward asylum seekers fleeing violence or persecution. Advocates of stricter enforcement point to concerns about border security, the strain of high numbers of border encounters on immigration courts and local resources, and the argument that immigration law should be consistently enforced. Congress has repeatedly attempted and failed to pass comprehensive immigration reform that would address the status of long term undocumented residents, border security, and future legal immigration levels together, leaving many of the specific questions, including the permanent status of DACA recipients, unresolved and subject to ongoing political and legal battles, closely connected to the broader patterns of political polarization discussed elsewhere in this unit.
